title: The Straits Claim
description: A two-stage historical negotiation about trade, law, and a disputed throne. As a junior interpreter, you help carry questions and advice between British officers and Johor leaders while a new port is being planned.
learningObjectives: Explain why the East India Company wanted a port at the Straits.
Describe the disputed succession in Johor in 1819.

player.name: You
player.role: Junior interpreter attached to Raffles' expedition
player.brief: You translate short exchanges, carry notes, and report what each side says. Your advice can shape how the expedition handles the legal problem over Singapore's ruler.

sharedContext.text: British merchants wanted a safe harbour near the Straits, and Raffles had orders to find one without provoking the Dutch. But Singapore belonged to Johor, and the Temenggong alone could not lawfully grant the land.

spans.quote: they had no safe harbour of their own at the southern end of the Straits of Malacca.
to establish a post at the southern end of the Straits but to avoid any collision with the Dutch
only the Sultan of Johor could lawfully grant land to the Company.

summary.text: Raffles led the expedition. He wanted a British station near the China Sea and later recognised Tengku Hussein as the stronger claimant to Johor.

needed a station commanding the entrance to the China Sea.
Raffles took the view that Tengku Hussein, as the elder son, had the stronger claim.

content.text: This note explains the dispute: Hussein was the elder son, but Abdul Rahman was installed while Hussein was away and later recognised by the Dutch.

spans.quote: When Sultan Mahmud Shah III of Johor died in 1812 he left two sons.
The younger, Tengku Abdul Rahman, was installed as Sultan in his absence with the support of the powerful Bugis faction at court, and this choice was later recognised by the Dutch.

content.text: The draft would let the Company establish a trading post at Singapore. In return, Hussein and the Temenggong would receive yearly payments.

spans.quote: The Company was permitted to establish a factory, or trading post, at Singapore.
In return the Sultan was to receive 5,000 Spanish dollars a year and the Temenggong 3,000 Spanish dollars a year.

endings.title: Treaty with Hussein
endings.summary: You help the expedition back Hussein's claim. The treaty is signed, and the new post begins with a stronger legal case than the first agreement allowed.

historicalOutcome.text: This matches the record. On 6 February 1819, Raffles, Hussein, and the Temenggong signed a treaty. The Company gained its trading post, Farquhar took charge, and Dutch protests followed.

endings.title: Post on a Weak Title
endings.summary: You help push ahead without settling the succession properly. A post may begin, but its legal basis stays weak and open to attack.

historicalOutcome.text: In the record, Raffles did not stop with the preliminary agreement. He recognised Hussein and signed a fuller treaty on 6 February 1819.

only the Sultan of Johor could lawfully grant land to the Company.

endings.divergence: Here the expedition acts on weaker authority than the sources say it used.
reflectionQuestions: Why was the Temenggong's signature not enough on its own?

endings.title: No Treaty Yet
endings.summary: You argue for caution. Talks pause, and the chance to secure Singapore now slips away while the succession dispute remains unresolved.

historicalOutcome.text: In the record, the British did not wait. Raffles recognised Hussein, signed the treaty on 6 February 1819, and the settlement later survived Dutch objections.

spans.quote: Raffles recognised him as Sultan Hussein Shah of Johor.
On 6 February 1819 a treaty was signed between the East India Company, represented by Raffles, Sultan Hussein and Temenggong Abdul Rahman.
The dispute was finally settled by the Anglo-Dutch Treaty of 1824, in which the Dutch withdrew their objection to the British presence in Singapore.

endings.divergence: This ending delays events that, in the record, moved very quickly in early February 1819.
reflectionQuestions: What are the strengths of waiting for clearer legitimacy?

endings.title: The Expedition Pulls Back
endings.summary: You help shut down the talks before a settlement is secured. The Company avoids an immediate clash, but it loses the opening at Singapore.

historicalOutcome.text: In the record, Raffles stayed long enough to secure the treaty, left Farquhar in charge, and the settlement remained despite uncertainty and protest.
